     UNEP: United Nations Environment Programme

         An agency of UN and coordinates its environmental activities, assisting developing
            countries in implementing environmentally sound policies. Started in 1972.

           Headquarter- Nairobi, Kenya

     IPCC- Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change





Treaties and Convention                                                                                                             1

Formed by UNEP and World Meteorological Organisation is a scientific and
            intergovernmental body under the auspices of the United Nations, with HQ at
           Geneva.

    UNCED- United Nations Conference on Environment and
     Development

                    It is also called the Rio Earth Summit 1992. It led to Agenda 21 dealing with
            sustainable development in 21st century and two legally binding agreements-
        UNFCCC and the CBD.

    UNFCCC- United Nations Framework Convention on
     Climate Change.

          The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (the Convention or
         UNFCCC) was adopted at the United Nations Headquarters, New York on the 9 May
            1992.

          The parties to the convention have met annually from 1995 in Conferences of the
             Parties (COP) to assess progress in dealing with climate change.

            At the 26th session of the Conference of the Parties (COP26) to the United Nations
          Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) held in Glasgow, United
           Kingdom, India adopted the Panchsheel targets:

              1. Reach 500 GW Non-fossil energy capacity by 2030.

              2. 50 per cent of its energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030.

              3. Reduction of total projected carbon emissions by one billion tonnes from now to
              2030.

              4. Reduction of the carbon intensity of the economy by 45 per cent by 2030, over
             2005 levels.

              5. Achieving the target of net zero emissions by 2070.

     Kyoto Protocol

                    It was concluded in 1997 and established legally binding obligations for developed
            countries to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions in the period 2008-2012. The
            protocol was adopted in Kyoto, Japan. Owing to a complex ratification process, it
            entered into force on 16 February 2005. The expiration date of the treaty was 2012.

          The Doha Amendment to the Kyoto Protocol (2012) was adopted for a second
          commitment period, starting in 2013 and lasting until 2020.

           However, the amendment could officially become active only after enough countries
            formally approved it. By 28 October 2020, 147 countries (Parties) had submitted

their approval documents, which met the required number for activation.

            So, the amendment officially entered into force on 31 December 2020 — even
           though the commitment period it covered (2013–2020) was already ending.

      Paris Agreement

          The Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015 to reduce greenhouse gas emissions,
           address global climate change, keep global temperature rise well below 2°C above
             pre-industrial levels, pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C, and promote adaptation
           measures.

                    It entered into force on 4 November 2016.

           Intended Nationally Determined Contributions - Under the Paris Agreement, each
           country sets and reports its own climate action targets to reduce global warming,
          and countries are expected to make future targets more ambitious over time.

      Problems with the Paris Agreement

          The agreement has been criticized for relying more on voluntary promises and goals
            than legally binding commitments. The United States, one of the largest greenhouse
           gas emitters after China, had also withdrawn from the agreement.

           According to UNEP, the emission reduction targets announced in November 2016
           could still lead to a global temperature rise of around 3°C above pre-industrial levels.

     Global Environment Facility

          The Global Environment Facility (GEF) was established on the eve of the 1992 Rio
            Earth Summit.

                    It is a financial mechanism for six multilateral conventions.

              Convention on Biological Diversity

             Minamata Convention on Mercury

              Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants

          UN Convention to Combat Desertification

          UN Framework Convention on Climate Change

             Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction

            Global Environment Facility HQ - Washington, DC, USA

     Convention on Biological Diversity

          The Convention on Biological Diversity was adopted on 22 May 1992 at the Nairobi
          Conference for the Adoption of the Agreed Text of the Convention on Biological
             Diversity.





Treaties and Convention                                                                                                             4

It was opened for signature at the United Nations Conference on Environment and
          Development (Rio Earth Summit) on 5 June 1992.

                    It entered into force on 29 December 1993.

           Cartagena Protocol, Nagoya Protocol, and Aichi Biodiversity Targets are the
           protocols/frameworks which operate under this convention.

      Cartagena Protocol

                    It was adopted on 29 January 2000 and entered into force on 11 September 2003.

          The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety is a safety agreement under the Convention on
             Biological Diversity.

                Its main goal is to make sure that genetically modified living organisms (called
            Living Modified Organisms or LMOs) are handled safely so they do not harm nature
            or human health.

            For example, genetically modified fish released into rivers may outcompete native
            species, disrupt ecosystems, reduce biodiversity, or introduce harmful traits that can
             affect wildlife, agriculture, and potentially human health.

     Nagoya Protocol

          The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing was adopted on 29 October
          2010 at the 10th Conference of the Parties (COP10) to the Convention on Biological
             Diversity in Nagoya, Japan, and entered into force on 12 October 2014.

          The Nagoya Protocol is an agreement under the Convention on Biological Diversity
             that ensures countries and communities sharing genetic resources also receive a
                fair share of the benefits earned from their use.

            For example, if a company uses medicinal plants from a country to develop
           medicines or cosmetics, the benefits such as profits, technology, or research
           support should be shared fairly with that country.

       Aichi Biodiversity Targets

          The Aichi Biodiversity Targets were 20 global biodiversity goals adopted in 2010
           under the Convention on Biological Diversity as part of the Strategic Plan for
             Biodiversity 2011–2020.

          These targets aimed to protect biodiversity, reduce environmental damage, and
           ensure sustainable use of natural resources by 2020. Countries were expected to
            create their own national biodiversity targets and action plans (NBSAPs) to achieve
           these global goals.

Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer,
     1985

                    It acts as a framework for the international efforts to protect the ozone layer.
           However, it does not include legally binding reduction goals for the use of CFCs.
          These are laid out in the accompanying Montreal Protocol in 1987.

          The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer is an
             international treaty designed to protect the ozone layer by phasing out the
            production of numerous substances that are responsible for ozone depletion like
         CFCs (Chlorofluorocarbon). This protocol is legally binding on the parties that
              ratified it.

             Adopted on 15 September 1987, the Protocol is to date the only UN treaty ever
                 that has been ratified by nearly every country on Earth.

          The Kigali Agreement of 2016 amends the 1987 Montreal Protocol and aims to
          phase out 85% of Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) by 2045.

               Global HFC use is projected to decline by 80–85% by 2047 under this
              agreement.

    RAMSAR Convention

          The Ramsar Convention, officially called the Convention on Wetlands of International
           Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat, is an international treaty that promotes
            the conservation and wise use of wetlands. It was adopted on 2 February 1971 in
           Ramsar, Iran.

           On February 2, the World Wetland Day is also observed.

          The Secretariat manages daily coordination and is based at the IUCN headquarters
              in Gland, Switzerland.

        UNESCO is the depository of the Convention and handles ratification and accession
           through its Director-General.

          The Montreux Record under the Ramsar Convention is a register of wetlands
            adversely affected by human activities. From India, Keoladeo National Park and
           Loktak Lake are included in this record.

     CITES- Convention on International Trade in Endangered
     Species of Wild Fauna and Flora

          CITES is an international agreement between governments that came into force on 1
            July 1975 to ensure that international trade in wild animals and plants does not
            threaten their survival. The trade here refers to international trade in wild animals,
             plants, and products made from them.





Treaties and Convention                                                                                                             6

It regulates trade through a licensing system for import, export, and re-export of
            protected species, and each member country must appoint authorities to manage
            permits and provide scientific advice.

          CITES is administered by the United Nations Environment Programme.

     IUCN- International Union for Conservation of Nature

           IUCN: International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources, formed
              in 1948. It is headquartered in Gland, Switzerland.

          IUCN is a membership Union of government and civil society organisations.

                    It publishes the Red Book- IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, having list of near
            threatened, vulnerable, endangered and critically endangered and extinct species.

     United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
    (UNCCD)

          The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994. It
         was established to combat desertification, land degradation, and the effects of
            drought, which threaten livelihoods, food security, and sustainable development.

     Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants,
     2001.

          The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants was adopted in 2001 in
           Stockholm, Sweden, and entered into force in 2004.

                    It is a global treaty aimed at protecting human health and the environment from
             persistent organic pollutants (POPs), which remain in the environment for long
            periods, spread widely, accumulate in living organisms, and cause harmful effects.

     Basel Convention on The Control of Transboundary
    Movement of Hazardous Waste

          The Basel Convention was adopted on 22 March 1989 and entered into force on 5
         May 1992. It was established to regulate and control the transboundary movement
          and disposal of hazardous wastes to protect human health and the environment.

     Rotterdam Convention

          The Rotterdam Convention was adopted in 1998 to promote shared responsibility
          and information exchange in the international trade of hazardous chemicals and
             pesticides, helping countries protect human health and the environment.





Treaties and Convention                                                                                                             7

Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030

          The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction was adopted on 18 March 2015 at
            the Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in Sendai, Japan, to
           reduce disaster risks and minimize losses to lives, livelihoods, health, and economic,
              social, cultural, and environmental assets.

     Wassenaar Arrangement

          The Wassenaar Arrangement was formally established in July 1996 to promote
            greater responsibility and transparency in the export of conventional weapons and
           dual-use goods and technologies, and to prevent destabilizing accumulations of
          such items

      Missile Technology Control Regime

          The Missile Technology Control Regime is an informal arrangement among countries
             to prevent the spread of missiles and related technologies capable of delivering
         Weapons of Mass Destruction and threatening international peace and security.

          The regime was formed in 1987 by the G-7 industrialized countries (Canada, France,
           Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, and the United States).

             India joined the treaty in 2016.

     Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons

          The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons was adopted on 12 June
           1968 at the United Nations in New York and entered into force on 5 March 1970. India
                is not a member.

          The treaty aims to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and related technology,
           promote peaceful use of nuclear energy, and achieve nuclear disarmament and
           complete global disarmament.

          The NPT is based on three pillars: non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, nuclear
           disarmament, and peaceful use of nuclear energy. It became part of international
           law in 1970.

     Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons

          The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons was approved by the United
            Nations in 2017 and came into force on 22 January 2021 to completely prohibit
            nuclear weapons and related activities, promote nuclear disarmament, and reduce
            the humanitarian and environmental risks caused by nuclear weapons.

     Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty





Treaties and Convention                                                                                                             8

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty was opened for signature in
          September 1996 to prohibit all nuclear weapon test explosions and other nuclear
            explosions anywhere in the world, with the aim of preventing nuclear weapons
           development and promoting nuclear disarmament.

      Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure

          The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure was launched by the Prime Minister
            of India at the UN Climate Action Summit on 23 September 2019 to promote resilient
             infrastructure systems against climate and disaster risks and support sustainable
           development.

          The CDRI Secretariat is based in New Delhi, India.

      International Solar Alliance

          The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was launched on 30th November 2015 in Paris,
            France, by Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi and the President of France
            François Hollande.

           ISA aims to collectively address common challenges in scaling up solar energy
         among 121 solar resource-rich countries located fully or partially between the Tropic
            of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn.

          The ISA is located at the National Institute of Solar Energy Campus in Gurugram.

             International Solar Alliance (ISA) is the first treaty-based international government
            organisation which is based in India.
